items.title: Microsoft MAI Code 2 and Code 2 Flash generally available in GitHub Copilot
facts: MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash are now generally available in GitHub Copilot.

MAI Code 2 Flash is a lightweight cost-efficient model for code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes, and rapid iteration.

items.title: Cursor details October security incident involving Fireworks key and malicious Claude Code extension
facts: An attacker obtained an access key Cursor had issued to Fireworks, which Fireworks exposed, and used it to copy limited coding agent traces.
The attacker placed malicious unauthorized copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension on the Cursor VS Code extension marketplace cache on October 29.
At most 5,000 users who requested specific cached versions potentially received the malicious build; Cursor says the incident is contained.

x_posts.author: @cursor_ai
x_posts.text: We’ve published an update on our recent security incident. See a detailed overview of what happened and our remediation steps here: https://cursor.com/blog/security-incident-update

x_posts.author: @koltregaskes2
x_posts.text:
Cursor has published its full write-up of the October security incident.

It started with an access key Cursor had issued to Fireworks, which Fireworks exposed. The attacker copied old coding agent traces, found a few unredacted credentials (under 0.01% of customers), reached some of Cursor's SaaS tools, then planted a fake Claude Code extension in Cursor's marketplace on 29 Oct.

Cursor says most customers weren't affected and it has contacted those who were.

items.title: Developers share Claude Code skills and persistent memory workflows for agent reuse
facts: Users describe saving work procedures as SKILL.md files in Claude Code and Codex for reuse by asking the agent to turn the current procedure into a Skill.

x_posts.author: @infoforinsta

x_posts.author: @younesbagh
x_posts.text:
Every project I work on makes Claude better at the next one.

Not because the model is actually learning.

I built it a “brain” that stores my decisions, experiments, research, and mistakes… then reads them before starting new work.

So every new session starts with what we already learned, instead of losing everything when the chat ends.

If you want to build the same system inside Claude Code, use this prompt:

Prompt:

“Build me a persistent second brain for Claude Code.

The goal is simple: every future session should benefit from decisions, experiments, research, and mistakes from previous sessions.

Create this structure:

- brain/decisions
- brain/results
- brain/research
- brain/lessons
- brain/topics
- brain/sources
- brain/index.md

Rules:

1. Before making any important recommendation or decision, search the brain for relevant previous decisions, results, lessons, and research.

2. If previous evidence contradicts the new recommendation, explicitly surface the contradiction before proceeding.

3. After any task that produces a meaningful decision, result, research finding, or reusable lesson, write it to the brain before marking the task complete.

4. Never overwrite historical decisions. If a new decision replaces an old one, mark the old decision as superseded and link both directions.

5. Every metric or number must include its date and source. Historical numbers are snapshots, not current truth.

6. Raw sources must remain immutable.

7. Avoid duplicated facts. Keep one canonical source and link to it from other files.

8. Never store passwords, API keys, personal customer data, emails, phone numbers, or private identifiers.

9. Maintain an index that summarizes the most important current knowledge and links to the underlying files.

10. Periodically audit the brain for contradictions, stale numbers, orphaned files, and lessons that should become permanent rules.

Also update CLAUDE.md so Claude automatically:

- reads the brain index at the start of…

items.title: Microsoft AI claims strong price-performance for MAI Code 2 vs GPT-6 and Claude on everyday coding benchmarks
facts: Averaged over four benchmarks (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1), MAI Code 2 gives 98% of the performance of GPT 6.1 Sol at 40% of the cost, and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5’s performance at 5% of the cost.
MAI Code 2 Flash offers comparable performance to GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 65% and 20% of the cost on day-to-day high-volume coding tasks.

x_posts.author: @MicrosoftAI
x_posts.text: MAI Code 2 Flash matches GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 on day-to-day, high-volume coding tasks, at 65% and 20% of the price, averaged across DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1 and SWE-Atlas.

items.title: Hot discussion on agentic coding evolution, review bottlenecks, and residual human role
facts: A widely engaged post outlines a timeline of AI coding developments and concludes that no-one is writing code anymore while the community figures out the implications.

x_posts.author: @mattpocockuk
x_posts.text:
A brief history of AI Coding since Nov 2025:

Nov 2025: Opus 4.5 releases, OpenClaw gets built
Dec 2025: community agrees that models get good enough to handle 95% of coding tasks
Jan 2026: Ralph loops get popular, early efforts on loops/orchestration
Feb: Everyone feels knackered, too much strategic decision-making, fears around cognitive debt begin
Mar: Skills explosion as community converges around easy-to-share processes (superpowers already ahead of the game here)
Apr: most SOTA devs haven't written a line of code in months
May: "The unreasonable effectiveness of HTML" - more interest in richer review surfaces
Jun: "Loop Engineering" wins vaguepost of the year, signals more hype around process
Jul: Every talk in every conference becomes "here is my software factory"
Aug: Opus 5 speaks incomprehensibly, interest in ASD-STE100 peaks
Sep: Grok Bot gets popular, more interest in long-running "manager" threads which retain context and delegate work
Oct: The promised speed gains haven't materialised, "dark factory" feels a long way off still
Nov: No-slop manifesto releases, reading the code still appears essential

TL;DR: no-one is writing code anymore, and we are still figuring out what that means
